content.title: What is March Madness? Explaining the NCAA men's basketball tournament
content.text: The NCAA men’s basketball tournament, also known as March Madness, sees school and university teams in the US take centre stage across three action-packed weeks. Here's how it works, how it started, and why the 68-team college showdown captivates fans every spring.Picture by 2025 Getty ImagesBy Will Imbo 13 March 2026 11:30 GMT+05 min readThis Tuesday (17 March), one of the most compelling sporting competitions in the United States begins with the opening games of the NCAA Division I men’s basketball tournament — better (and more aptly) known as March Madness. Each year, the three-week, 68-team single-elimination tournament produces some of the most memorable moments in basketball. From George Mason's Cinderella to the Final Four in 2006 to a certain freshman named Michael Jordan hitting the championship-winning shot for North Carolina in 1982, March Madness is the stage where upsets happen, dreams are realised (and shattered), and legends are made. But what exactly is March Madness? How did it become a phenomenon in North America and beyond? And how does the NCAA tournament actually work? We’ve got the answers below.Picture by Sam Hodde/Getty ImagesHow March Madness began The NCAA Division I men’s basketball tournament dates back to 1939, when it was first held as an eight-team competition in the USA. Oregon won that inaugural national title, beating Ohio State 46-33 in the championship game. Over time, the field expanded and the tournament gradually became a much larger part of the North American sporting calendar, eventually growing into the 68-team event seen today. Even the phrase March Madness has a longer history than many casual viewers realise. According to NCAA.com, it was first used in a basketball context by Illinois high school official Henry V. Porter in 1939, but it did not become closely associated with the NCAA men’s tournament until CBS broadcaster Brent Musburger used it during the 1982 tournament. Since then, the name has become inseparable from the event. The tournament’s growth was gradual rather than immediate. What began as a modest championship evolved into a national showcase for US college basketball, helped by expansion, television coverage and the simple appeal of a knockout format. By the time the field expanded to 64 teams in 1985, and then to 68 in 2011 with the addition of the First Four, March Madness had already become one of the most recognisable annual events in USA sport.Picture by Sam Hodde/Getty ImagesSAN ANTONIO, TEXAS - APRIL 07: The Florida Gators celebrate after defeating the Houston Cougars in the 2025 National Championship.How the NCAA 'March Madness' tournament works March Madness is the national championship tournament for men’s college basketball in the United States. More specifically, it features teams from NCAA Division I — the top level of NCAA competition — rather than every university team in the country. Division I has more than 360 member schools, but only 68 teams qualify for the tournament each year. Those 68 places are not awarded simply on ranking alone. Some teams qualify automatically by winning their conference tournaments, while others are chosen by the NCAA selection committee as at-large bids. On Selection Sunday, the committee reveals the full bracket, including which teams have qualified and where they have been seeded. The format itself is fairly simple. The tournament begins with the First Four, which reduces the field from 68 teams to 64. From there, the remaining teams are placed into a knockout bracket: lose once, and your season is over. The rounds then move from the first round to the second round, Sweet 16, Elite Eight, Final Four, and finally the national championship game. For the 2026 men’s tournament, the bracket will be revealed on 15 March, with the First Four on 17–18 March and the first round on 19–20 March. The Final Four will be played in Indianapolis on 4 April, before the championship game on 6 April.Why the "Madness" grips fans every year The simplest explanation lies in the format. March Madness is easy to understand but almost impossible to predict. A team can dominate its conference all winter, only to see its season end in the space of a single 40-minute game. At the same time, a lower-seeded outsider can catch fire for a night and suddenly become the story of the tournament. That unpredictability is what fuels the upsets that define March Madness — and why the idea of the “Cinderella” team, an underdog making an unlikely run, has become one of the tournament’s most enduring traditions. Its history is full of moments that have outlived the seasons around them. In 1982, a young Michael Jordan hit the shot that helped North Carolina beat Georgetown for the national title.Picture by Malcolm Emmons-USA TODAY SportsMar 29, 1982; New Orleans, LA, USA; North Carolina Tar Heels guard Michael Jordan (23) in action against Georgetown during the 1982 Final Four Championship game at the Superdome. The Tar Heels defeated the Hoyas 63-62, with Jordan hitting the game-winning jump shot.... Read moreA year later, NC State completed one of the tournament’s most famous Cinderella runs when Lorenzo Charles’ last-second dunk sealed a 54-52 win over heavily favoured Houston. In 2018, UMBC became the first No. 16 seed to beat a No. 1 seed in the men’s tournament, defeating Virginia. And in 2016, Kris Jenkins hit a championship-winning buzzer-beater to give Villanova the title over North Carolina.Picture by Jared C. Tilton/Getty ImagesUMBC's 74-54 victory over the Virginia Cavaliers during the first round of the 2018 March Madness tournament has gone down in college basketball folklore.Another reason March Madness resonates so widely is that fans do not just watch it — they participate in it. Every year, millions fill out brackets and try to predict the full path of the tournament, even though the NCAA says the odds of creating a perfect bracket are 1 in 9.2 quintillion. That challenge turns even casual viewers into active participants, giving them a reason to care about games and teams they might not otherwise follow closely. Then there is the ritual around the tournament itself. From the bracket reveal on Selection Sunday to the constant churn of games and the emergence of unexpected stars, March Madness has developed traditions that make it feel like more than a championship, the whole thing televised and covered in a minute detail that put new pressures on collegiate teams and student athletes who may have never faced such attention before. That, ultimately, is the appeal. March Madness combines clarity and chaos: a simple bracket, a ruthless format, and just enough unpredictability to make every game feel like it could become part of the tournament’s history.Michael Jordan: Being part of 1992 Dream Team was "highlight of my career"Basketball legend Michael Jordan looks back on the USA's historical triumph in the men's competition at Barcelona 1992.
